title: E-commerce and Marketing Automation
summary: E-commerce and marketing are two of the biggest sources of paid automation work, because online businesses live and die by how efficiently they turn events into actions, so these workflows are worth mastering. On the e-commerce side, store platforms
content:
# E-commerce and Marketing Automation ##### The reminder that went to people who had already paid A D2C skincare brand launched an abandoned-cart automation. The logic seemed obvious: someone starts checkout, wait an hour, send "You left something behind!" The morning after launch, their support inbox filled with variations of the same message: *"I already bought this yesterday. Why are you telling me my cart is abandoned?"* Several customers, mid-purchase when the email arrived, assumed their order had failed and bought again. Refunds followed. So did a small pile of unsubscribes. The bug was one missing step: nobody checked, at the moment of sending, whether the order had since been completed. It is the single most common mistake in e-commerce automation, and it teaches the governing principle of this whole domain — **e-commerce automations act on people's money and inboxes, so the cost of being wrong is unusually high.** E-commerce and marketing are also two of the largest sources of paid automation work, because online businesses live or die by how efficiently they turn events into actions. This day is where a lot of freelance income comes from. ##### Store platform automation **Shopify** dominates and has an excellent event model. The webhook topics you will use constantly: `orders/create`, `orders/paid`, `orders/fulfilled`, `orders/cancelled`, `checkouts/create`, `checkouts/update`, `customers/create`, `refunds/create`, and `inventory_levels/update`. **WooCommerce** (WordPress) is huge in India and Southeast Asia because it is free and self-hosted. It exposes a REST API and webhooks, though setup is more manual and reliability depends on the host's server. Whichever platform, the same automations recur: order confirmation and invoice, inventory sync, shipping notifications, review requests after delivery, low-stock alerts, VIP-customer flagging, and reporting. Two technical realities to internalize. First, **order data is nested**: `line_items` is an array, so you almost always need an iterator — the three-item order problem from Make day, in production. Second, **`orders/create` fires before payment confirms**. Automating fulfilment on `create` rather than `paid` is how people ship goods for orders that were never paid for. ##### Payment events with Stripe Stripe's webhook model is the cleanest example in the industry and worth learning as a template for all payment integrations. The events that matter: | Event | Meaning | Typical action | |---|---|---| | `checkout.session.completed` | Checkout finished | Fulfil the order — the canonical trigger | | `payment_intent.succeeded` | Payment captured | Confirm, log revenue | | `payment_intent.payment_failed` | Card declined | Alert, prompt a retry | | `charge.refunded` | Refund issued | Reverse fulfilment, update records | | `customer.subscription.created/updated/deleted` | Subscription lifecycle | Grant or revoke access | | `invoice.payment_failed` | Recurring charge failed | Dunning sequence | Three Stripe-specific practices that generalize to every payment provider: **Verify the signature.** Stripe signs every webhook. Never trust an unverified payload — someone could post a fake `payment_intent.succeeded` and get free goods. ```python import os, stripe from flask import Flask, request app = Flask(__name__) ENDPOINT_SECRET = os.environ["STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET"] @app.post("/webhooks/stripe") def stripe_webhook(): payload = request.get_data() # RAW body, not parsed JSON sig = request.headers.get("Stripe-Signature", "") try: event = stripe.Webhook.construct_event(payload, sig, ENDPOINT_SECRET) except (ValueError, stripe.error.SignatureVerificationError): return "invalid", 400 # reject forgeries if event["type"] == "checkout.session.completed": session = event["data"]["object"] # idempotency: Stripe retries, so guard on the event id if already_processed(event["id"]): return "duplicate ignored", 200 enqueue_fulfilment( order_ref=session["id"], email=session["customer_details"]["email"], amount=session["amount_total"] / 100, # paise -> rupees currency=session["currency"].upper(), ) mark_processed(event["id"]) return "ok", 200 # respond fast ``` **Respond immediately, process afterwards.** Stripe expects a `2xx` within seconds and retries for up to three days otherwise. Do the heavy work asynchronously. **Be idempotent.** Retries mean the same event arrives multiple times. Guard on the event ID — as above — or you will fulfil one order twice. Also note `amount_total` is in the smallest currency unit: `499800` means ₹4,998.00. Payment APIs use integers for money precisely to avoid floating-point errors, and forgetting to divide is a memorable bug. ##### Email marketing automation Mailchimp, Klaviyo, Brevo, ConvertKit and ActiveCampaign all share a model: **contacts** live in **lists/audiences**, carry **tags** and **custom fields**, and can be enrolled in **sequences** (automated series of emails). Your automation's job is almost always the same: keep the contact record accurate and correctly tagged, then let the marketing tool handle the sending. Tags are the interface between your automation and the marketing team's campaigns — `customer`, `first-purchase`, `vip`, `abandoned-cart`, `product-skincare`, `city-pune`. The pattern from CRM day applies exactly: **search-then-update-or-create on a normalized email**, never blind create. Most marketing APIs offer an upsert; Mailchimp's uses an MD5 hash of the lowercased email as the member ID, which is effectively an upsert key. Three rules specific to email, and they carry legal weight: 1. **Never add someone to marketing without consent.** A purchase is consent for transactional email (receipts, shipping) but not necessarily for promotional campaigns. Track consent as a field. 2. **Honour unsubscribes everywhere.** If someone unsubscribes in Mailchimp, your automation must not re-add them from the CRM on the next sync. Check status before writing. 3. **Keep transactional and marketing separate.** Receipts must always send; promotions must respect preferences. ##### Abandoned cart and follow-up sequences Abandoned-cart recovery is the highest-ROI e-commerce automation in existence — typical recovery rates run around 10–15% of abandoned carts, which on real revenue is substantial. The structure, with the bug from the opening story fixed: ```mermaid flowchart TD A[checkouts/create or update
with email captured] --> B[Store checkout in DB
id, email, items, value, status=open] B --> C[Wait 1 hour] C --> D{Order completed since?
re-check the database NOW} D -->|yes| X[Exit — do not send] D -->|no| E{Consent + not unsubscribed?} E -->|no| X E -->|yes| F[Email 1: gentle reminder
with cart contents] F --> G[Wait 23 hours] G --> H{Order completed?} H -->|yes| X H -->|no| I[Email 2: social proof / FAQ] I --> J[Wait 48 hours] J --> K{Order completed?} K -->|yes| X K -->|no| L[Email 3: small discount code] L --> M[Mark sequence complete] ``` The critical design detail — and what the assignment asks about — is the **re-check before every send**. The condition must be evaluated *at send time*, not at enrolment time, because the customer may have completed the purchase during the delay. Three complementary techniques: 1. **Query current state at send time.** Look up the checkout's status in your database or via the platform API immediately before sending. This is the essential one. 2. **Cancel on completion.** When `orders/create` fires with a matching checkout token or email, set the stored record's status to `converted` so every downstream check exits. 3. **Suppression window.** Never send a cart reminder to someone who purchased in the last 24 hours, whatever the trigger says. Add practical guards: only enrol checkouts above a minimum value, cap frequency so one person cannot receive multiple sequences in a week, and always exclude anyone who unsubscribed. The same *wait-then-recheck* pattern powers post-purchase sequences (thank you → shipping → review request 5 days after **delivery**, not after order) and win-back campaigns (no purchase in 90 days → re-engagement). ##### Syncing customers across tools A typical stack has the store, a payment processor, a CRM, an email tool, a helpdesk and a data warehouse. The same person exists in all six. Design principles that keep this sane: - **Pick one source of truth per field.** The store owns purchase history; the email tool owns subscription status; the CRM owns sales stage. Write each field from its owner only. - **Use email as the join key**, normalized to lowercase and trimmed — everywhere, every time. - **Prefer one-way sync** from the source of truth outward. Two-way sync invites the infinite loops from CRM day. - **Sync deliberately, not continuously.** Real-time for purchase events; a nightly batch for enrichment and cleanup. - **Log every sync** so you can answer "why does this contact have that tag?" ##### Common pitfalls - **Sending cart reminders to people who purchased** — re-check at send time. - **Triggering fulfilment on order creation instead of payment.** - **Not verifying webhook signatures** on payment events. - **Missing idempotency** — duplicate orders, duplicate emails, duplicate charges logged. - **Money as floats** — use integers in the smallest unit, or decimals. - **Only mapping `line_items[0]`** — the multi-item order bug. - **Ignoring refunds and cancellations** — your revenue reporting and email sequences both drift. - **Adding customers to marketing without consent**, or re-adding unsubscribers on sync. - **Testing with live keys** — every payment provider gives you test mode; use it. - **Currency and time-zone confusion** in reporting. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: build an automation triggered by a **Stripe (or store) payment event** that logs the order, sends a **personalized confirmation email**, and **adds or updates the customer** in an email-marketing tool with the right tag. Use Stripe's test mode and its CLI (`stripe listen --forward-to `) to replay real event payloads at your workflow — it is the best possible way to test payment automations safely. The mini project is a **mini e-commerce suite**: on a new order, generate an invoice and confirmation; add the customer to a **post-purchase sequence**; and build an **abandoned-checkout follow-up** using a delay and a filter — keeping the customer record synced across CRM and email tool. Build the re-check into the abandoned-cart flow from the start and test it explicitly: enrol a checkout, complete the purchase during the delay, and confirm no email is sent. That test is the deliverable. For the assignment, **diagram the abandoned-cart automation end to end** — trigger, delay, condition, actions — and explain how you prevent sending to customers who completed their purchase. Name all three mechanisms: re-query state at send time, cancel the sequence on the order event, and apply a recent-purchase suppression window. Explaining *why* the check must happen at send time rather than enrolment time is the part that shows real understanding. ##### Key takeaways - E-commerce automations touch money and inboxes, so correctness matters more here than almost anywhere else. - Trigger fulfilment on payment events (`orders/paid`, `checkout.session.completed`), never on order creation, and always iterate over `line_items`. - Verify payment webhook signatures, respond fast then process, and guard on the event ID for idempotency — money in payment APIs is an integer in the smallest unit. - Keep marketing contacts accurate with search-then-upsert on a normalized email, respect consent and unsubscribes, and keep transactional email separate from promotional. - In any delayed sequence, re-evaluate the condition at send time — that single rule is what stops abandoned-cart emails reaching customers who already paid.
